hints: Look at what 1.39 in Table 3.1 really means - it is 1.39 cases for every 100000 people in Ethiopia in 2009, not the total.
Think how to scale that rate up to the whole Ethiopian population of 84838000 - what fraction or multiplication links 100000 to that total?
walkthrough:
Understand What Per 100000 Means**
The table does not give you the total cases. It tells you that if you took any 100000 Ethiopians in 2009, about 1.39 of them had measles. To get the real total you must multiply this rate by how many groups of 100000 are in the whole population.

Scale Up To The Full Population**
Number of 100000 groups = $84838000 / 100000 = 848.38$. Then actual cases = $1.39 \times 848.38 = 1179.24$. People must be whole numbers, so round down to $1179$ cases. This matches the check values: Chad $1.45 \times 113.71 = 165$ and Eritrea $1.48 \times 55.58 = 82$.
Final answer: $1.39 \times \frac{84838000}{100000} = 1.39 \times 848.38 = 1179$ cases (to whole person).

hints: Compare the 2009 populations of Chad, Eritrea and Ethiopia - they are very different sizes, so what would happen if you only compared total case numbers like 165 vs 82?
Now look at their 2009 rates per 100000 - 1.45, 1.48 and 1.39 - what does their similarity tell you that the raw totals hide?
Think beyond one year - why would a rate be more useful for judging if disease is getting worse or better in the same country over time, or for judging how serious it is?
walkthrough:
The Population Size Problem**
Chad has about 11 million, Eritrea about 5.5 million and Ethiopia about 84.8 million people. A big country will almost always have more total cases just because it has more people. So 1179 cases in Ethiopia sounds much worse than 82 in Eritrea, but that is misleading.

How Standardising Solves It**
Dividing by population and expressing as per 100000 normalises the data. It shows the proportion affected. In 2009 Chad 1.45, Eritrea 1.48 and Ethiopia 1.39 per 100000 are almost identical. That tells you the severity or risk to an individual is very similar in all three.

Why This Is More Useful**
This allows fair comparison between countries and fair tracking over time if a population grows or shrinks. You can judge if disease is spreading, dying out or under control, and whether control measures are working, rather than being fooled by population size.

Final answer: Per 100000 gives proportion/percentage affected and allows valid comparison between countries and over time within a country, taking population size into account. E.g. Chad, Eritrea and Ethiopia have very different populations but similar 2009 rates of 1.45, 1.48 and 1.39 per 100000, showing similar severity despite 165, 82 and 1179 actual cases. Larger populations will naturally have more cases.

walkthrough:
Find Data That Fits Protection**
Gambia stays at about 90-95% vaccinated in Fig. 3.1 from 2003 to 2012 and Table 3.1 shows 0.00, 0.12, 0.00, 0.00 cases per 100000. Eritrea stays at 95-99% and stays low at 1.48, 0.89, 0.81 except 3.16 in 2012. High coverage pairs with low incidence, as expected if vaccine protects.

Spot Partial Support**
Chad vaccination rises from about 27% in 2008 to about 64% in 2012. Cases are low in 2009 at 1.45, 2010 at 1.66 and 2012 at 0.96. Central African Republic falling vaccination still has a high case year in 2011 at 15.31, which fits.

Find Data That Breaks The Pattern**
Many data do not fit. Niger vaccination rises from ~49% to ~73% but cases go 5.23 to 2.34 to 4.67 to 1.59 - up and down. Ethiopia vaccination rises from ~43% to ~66% but cases rise from 1.39 in 2009 to 4.86 in 2010. Chad jumps from 1.66 in 2010 to 71.6 in 2011 despite rising vaccination. Central African Republic has falling vaccination yet low cases of 0.26 and 0.05 in 2009-2010. So protection is not consistently shown, possibly because coverage is below ~90% needed for herd immunity.

Final answer: Support: Gambia (and Eritrea) maintain high % vaccinated ~90-95% throughout and have low cases, e.g. Gambia 0.00-0.12 per 100000; Chad from 2008 increasing vaccination shows low cases 1.45, 1.66, 0.96 in 2009, 2010, 2012. Not support: Niger/Ethiopia/Chad show generally increasing vaccination but cases fluctuate/increase, e.g. Niger 2.34 to 4.67 in 2010-2011, Ethiopia 1.39 to 4.86 in 2009-2010, Chad 1.66 to 71.6 in 2010-2011; Central African Republic decreasing vaccination but low cases 0.26, 0.05 in 2009-2010.

walkthrough: Current-syllabus full-credit route: Use the supplied intensive global vaccination programme and general control principles. A high proportion immunised by mass vaccination reduces transmission; easy administration and straightforward training allow the programme to reach people effectively. These are two separately accepted official points, sufficient for the two marks. The original historical walkthrough below gives additional accepted alternatives; its smallpox-specific vaccine facts are optional historical extensions, not essential current-syllabus recall.

A Vaccine Suited To Global Use**
Smallpox vaccine was freeze-dried and heat stable, so it did not need a constant cold chain in hot countries. One dose gave long-lasting immunity with no boosters, and the same stable antigens could be used everywhere with mass coverage. It was also easy to give with simple training.

A Disease Suited To Containment**
Infected people were easy to recognise from the rash, so teams could use ring vaccination - tracing and vaccinating all contacts around each case. Smallpox is also less infectious than measles, so a lower percentage coverage was enough for herd immunity.

Final answer: Any two: high proportion immunised by mass vaccination; one dose gives very long-lived immunity with no boosters needed; same vaccine/antigens used throughout; heat-stable freeze-dried vaccine with long shelf life; easy to administer with little training; ring vaccination by contact tracing; easy to identify infected people; lower herd immunity threshold as less infectious than measles.

hints: Focus on two words - is immunity made by your own body or given ready-made, and does it come from natural infection or a medical intervention?
walkthrough:
Active And Artificial**
Active means your own B lymphocytes respond to the measles antigens in the vaccine and make your own antibodies and memory cells. Artificial means the antigens were introduced deliberately by vaccination, not by natural infection.
Final answer: Active artificial immunity.

walkthrough:
Materials And Storage Costs**
You must pay to make or buy the vaccine, plus disposables like syringes, needles and gloves. You must pay for secure storage and refrigeration to keep the cold chain so the vaccine stays effective.

Delivery And People Costs**
You must pay for transport of vaccine and staff, wages and training for health workers, setting up camps in remote areas, plus record keeping, contact tracing and advertising to inform the public.

Final answer: Any two: cost of manufacturing/purchasing vaccine; syringes, needles, gloves and equipment; storage and security; refrigeration/maintaining cold chain; transport of vaccine and workers; wages/training of health workers; record keeping/contact tracing; advertising/education; research/development; setting up vaccination camps.
